title: Doubt
hook: doubt is not unbelief; Thomas doubted and was still an apostle

segments.voice: Yesterday, grief: Jesus wept at the tomb of Lazarus, and the crowd said, behold how he loved him. Your line was grief is love. Whose name did you say out loud? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

Thomas missed the meeting. On the evening of the day the tomb is found empty, the disciples are behind locked doors, and the risen Jesus stands among them. Thomas isn't there. When he gets back, the others are almost shouting: we have seen the Lord. And Thomas says no. Not unless he sees it himself. "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe." For a whole week he's the one in the room who can't say yes. Today: doubt.

First, what happens next. After eight days the doors are shut again, and this time Thomas is there. Jesus comes, and he goes straight to him. No scolding speech. He offers exactly what Thomas asked for: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing." The doubter gets a visit of his own. Second, what Thomas says. The text never says he touched the wounds. It says he answered, "My Lord and my God." The man remembered for doubting calls Jesus, plainly, both Lord and God. The doubt didn't disqualify him; it was the road he took to get there. Third, he isn't alone. In the last scene of Matthew's Gospel, the disciples meet Jesus on a mountain, and the text says, "they worshipped him: but some doubted." Worship and doubt in the same sentence, the same crowd. And Jesus sends all of them out anyway. In Mark, a desperate father brings his son to Jesus and cries out, "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Both at once, said in one breath, and Jesus heals the boy. Last, where Thomas went. Tradition says he traveled east and carried the faith as far as India, and some Christians in India keep that story as their own. The doubter, in that telling, became a messenger to a far country. So some Christians make a distinction here. Unbelief walks away. Doubt stays in the room and asks to see. Doubt belongs.
screen: `TRADITION SAYS: ALL THE WAY TO INDIA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one doubt kindly. Settle, and breathe. Let one honest question come up, about God, about faith, about a story you've heard, or about yourself. Don't argue with it. Don't rush to answer it. Just name it, in one plain sentence, the way Thomas did: here's what I can't say yes to yet. Then breathe beside it, the way you'd sit beside a friend who's unsure. If you pray, you can borrow the father's words: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. The bell holds the time.
Doubt. An honest question that stays in the room. Thomas doubted, was visited, and spoke the words my Lord and my God.
Your line: doubt belongs. Today, when someone admits they're unsure about something that matters, don't fix it. Thank them for saying it. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Christians remember Thomas on his feast day and read his story in church on the Sunday after Easter in some traditions; some churches hold groups where questions and doubts are spoken aloud, and the father's prayer from Mark is prayed as a short prayer of its own.

fork.setup: you're Thomas. your friends swear they've seen Jesus alive, and you weren't there. what do you say?
options: unless I see the nails and touch his side, I won't believe.
fork.reveal: Thomas asks to see for himself. he stays with the others for a week, still unsure, and Jesus comes back for him.

original.note: Greek: faithless, unbelieving, in "be not faithless, but believing." the opposite is πιστός, believing.

trapdoor: what you thought: doubting Thomas was the disciple who failed.
what it means: Thomas asked to see, Jesus came back for him, and he spoke the words my Lord and my God.
what a scholar hears: Jesus says be not apistos but pistos, not faithless but believing. the text never says Thomas touched the wounds, and his answer calls Jesus Lord and God.

notes: 'Eight days later' is from John 20:26 ('after eight days'); 'for a whole week' is the lesson's paraphrase of the same. Confirm.
Thomas's mission to India and the name 'Saint Thomas Christians' are given as tradition; confirm phrasing.
Avoided calling 'My Lord and my God' the Gospel's boldest confession under the claims rule.
'Some Christians make a distinction' between doubt and unbelief; confirm fairness.
howItsDone: Thomas Sunday / Second Sunday of Easter reading 'in some traditions'; confirm.
Practice offers Mark 9:24 as a line to borrow 'if you pray'; it is scripture, not a new prayer.

Editor pass: 'eight days later' now follows the KJV's 'after eight days'; 'at the very end of Matthew's Gospel' softened to 'in the last scene'; the uncited present-tense claim about Saint Thomas Christians reworded as 'some Christians in India keep that story as their own', still under 'tradition says'.
Audit: 'the evening after the empty tomb' could be heard as the next evening; John 20:19 says 'the same day at evening', so the hook now says the evening of the day the tomb is found empty.
